messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 19
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Counselor
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 67

Here is a clinical vignette based on the provided information.

---

Marco is a 19-year-old man who presents as serious and thoughtful, his words carefully chosen as if he is still parsing through a dense, painful text. He’s been with his partner, Lena, for two years, and he mentions her frequently, not as a source of drama, but as a quiet anchor. He works as a peer support counselor at a community center, a job he took on just three months ago, and it is this role that seems to define his current struggle.

The story begins six months ago, at the end of his senior year of high school. Marco was a distance runner, lean and disciplined. He started feeling a persistent, low-grade fatigue, then a strange, unexplained bruise on his thigh. He ignored it, chalking it up to training. Then came the night he woke up drenched in sweat, his heart hammering so hard he thought it would break his ribs. His mother, a nurse, took one look at him and drove him to the ER. Within hours, his world collapsed into a diagnosis: Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia.

The narrative of his life was violently interrupted. The next four months were a blur of hospital rooms, the chemical sting of port-a-cath insertions, and the bone-deep ache of chemotherapy. He describes the treatment not as a fight, but as a slow drowning. He remembers the specific, metallic taste in his mouth, the way the fluorescent lights in the oncology ward hummed a constant, low note of dread. He remembers Lena’s hand, always cold, always there. He remembers his mother’s face, a mask of forced calm.

Now, Marco is in remission. His hair has grown back, a soft brown fuzz. He is back in the world. But the world feels wrong. He tells me that he is not afraid of the cancer returning, not in the way people expect. *That* fear is a rational, distant thundercloud. The terror he lives with is immediate and physical.

It manifests in his body. Two weeks ago, while sitting in a coffee shop, he felt a faint, familiar ache in his lower back. His mind did not think, “It’s probably just how I slept.” Instead, his body reacted. His throat closed. His vision tunneled. He was instantly back in the hospital bed, the sheets rough, the IV pump beeping its relentless rhythm. He had to excuse himself and sit in the bathroom on the cold tile floor for twenty minutes, his hands shaking, waiting for the feeling to pass. He knows it was a panic attack, but the knowing doesn’t stop the visceral terror.

His work as a counselor is a daily exposure therapy he never signed up for. He listens to teenagers talk about their parents’ divorces, their social anxiety, their fights with friends. He is good at it; he is empathetic and calm. But every story of pain, every mention of a hospital, every time a client describes a feeling of being trapped, his own chest tightens. He finds himself holding his breath. He has started to dread certain shifts, a feeling of profound guilt washing over him because he is supposed to be the one who helps.

At home, with Lena, he is different. He is hypervigilant. He checks her breathing at night, a compulsive habit he cannot explain. He has a new, terrifying fear of her being hurt, of being separated from her. He replays the night of his diagnosis in his head, not as a memory, but as a warning. He feels a constant, low-level pressure in his sinuses and his joints, scanning his own body for the first sign of betrayal. He tells me, his voice flat, “My own body is a haunted house. I live in it, but I don’t feel safe here anymore.” He is present in the room, but a part of him is still in that hospital bed, listening to the hum of the fluorescent light.
